title: Incident: Cloudflare outage, July 2019
objective: Follow Cloudflare's write-up of 2 July 2019: how one firewall rule with a bad regular expression used up CPU worldwide in minutes, and what changed so it can't happen that way again.

sources.title: Cloudflare Blog: Details of the Cloudflare outage on July 2, 2019 (John Graham-Cumming): "a regular expression that backtracked enormously and exhausted CPU used for HTTP/HTTPS serving"

simplifies: Simplified to its key moments from Cloudflare's own write-up (all times UTC). The write-up's long appendix on how regular expressions backtrack is reduced to one step.

steps.caption: Cloudflare's firewall (WAF) has managed rules that block attacks. A new rule was written, merged and tested: "With the tests passing, TeamCity automatically began deploying the change at 13:42."

WAF rules don't go through the usual staged rollout (dogfood, then pilot, then canary sites): "by design, the WAF doesn't use this process because of the need to respond rapidly to threats." Rules reach every server within seconds.

The rule's regular expression "backtracked enormously and exhausted CPU used for HTTP/HTTPS serving": CPU spiked to nearly 100% across Cloudflare's servers, and websites behind Cloudflare failed to load.

predict.prompt: The rule contains a regular expression that backtracks enormously. It reaches every server within seconds. What happens next?

options.text: Only a few servers slow down
options.explanation: There was no staged rollout, so every server got the rule together.

options.text: CPU on servers across the network jumps to nearly 100%, and sites stop loading
options.explanation: Right. Every server ran the same slow pattern on its traffic at once.

options.text: The tests would already have caught it
options.explanation: The tests had passed; checking each rule's CPU use (performance profiling) was one of the changes added afterwards.

steps.caption: Engineers proposed a "global terminate": a mechanism built in to disable one component worldwide, here the whole WAF.
They "executed the global WAF termination at 14:07", and "by 14:09 traffic levels and CPU were back to expected levels worldwide."
"At 14:52 we were 100% satisfied that we understood the cause and had a fix in place", and the WAF was turned back on.

Changes Cloudflare listed: bring back the CPU protection that had been removed; inspect all 3,868 rules; add performance profiling to the tests; move to a regex engine with run-time guarantees; and roll out rules in stages, keeping an emergency global option for active attacks.

quiz.prompt: Why did one rule take down sites worldwide within minutes?

options.text: The rule blocked all traffic on purpose
options.explanation: It used up CPU; it wasn't meant to block everything.
The cause was software: one regular expression.

options.text: WAF rules were pushed to every server at once, and the rule used up CPU on all of them
options.explanation: Right. Speed of rollout, normally a strength against attacks, spread the failure everywhere.

quiz.prompt: Which change most directly stops the next bad rule from reaching every server at once?

options.explanation: Helpful, but people will still make mistakes; staging limits the damage when they do.
Catastrophic backtracking can use up any amount of CPU.

options.text: Rolling rules out in stages, with an emergency global option kept for attacks
options.explanation: Right. A bad rule then hurts a small part of the network first, where it's noticed.
